individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: Omni-View is a unified multimodal model for 3D scenes that combines an understanding model with two generation modules (texture and geometry) to jointly perform scene understanding, novel view synthesis, and geometry estimation. The key idea is that generation tasks—especially geometry estimation and autoregressive novel view synthesis—can improve 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. The model is built on BAGEL-7B and trained in two stages: first jointly on understanding and generation objectives with a dense-to-sparse curriculum over reference views, then finetuning the generation modules with RGB-Depth-Pose joint learning. Experiments show state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench (55.4), strong performance on SQA3D/ScanQA/ScanRefer, and competitive novel view synthesis and scene generation results on Re10k.
Strengths: The idea of using generation to improve understanding in 3D scenes is timely and relevant, and the paper provides both architectural and training-strategy innovations (texture vs. geometry separation, dense-to-sparse reference curriculum, autoregressive generation).
Empirical results are impressive, especially the large gain on VSI-Bench (55.4 vs. 46.3 for BAGEL-7B-FT) and competitive generation quality in Table 3.
Ablations (Tables 4-7) decompose the contributions of texture and geometry modules, autoregressive generation, dense-to-sparse training, and stage 2, giving useful insights into the design choices.
The model avoids explicit 3D input, which makes it applicable to real-world scenarios where 3D scans are unavailable.
The paper includes a qualitative analysis and acknowledges some limitations (e.g., synthetic depth maps, grounding ability).
Weaknesses: A major confound exists in the main comparisons: BAGEL-7B-FT is likely trained only on understanding data, while Omni-View also uses 61k additional video clips from Re10k. The reported gains could stem partly from extra data/compute, not from the 'generation facilitates understanding' mechanism. Ablations do not control for data amount (e.g., a baseline trained on the same generation data but only with an understanding objective).

Model-size mismatch in comparisons: several strong baselines (VG-LLM-4B, Spatial-MLLM-4B) are 4B-parameter models, while Omni-View-7B has 7B parameters. This weakens the claim of state-of-the-art status.

The geometry module's actual depth and pose estimation accuracy is never directly evaluated. Since training uses synthetic depth maps from Voyager, the paper's claim of 'explicit geometric constraints' is not well validated, and the ablation shows only limited improvement in absolute distance tasks.

The paper has many typos and formatting errors (e.g., 'forzen', 'randon mask', 'donate' for denote, broken equations, garbled table formatting). These issues significantly hurt clarity and reproducibility.

The ablation studies use a 'VSI-Bench (subset)' that is not clearly defined; if this subset overlaps with the test set used for the main VSI-Bench evaluation, repeated ablations could lead to overfitting.

In Section 4.2.3, the text states 'Omni-View shows only slight improvements over popular scene generation models,' but Table 3 shows large improvements in LPIPS (0.114 vs. 0.175) and SSIM, which is contradictory and confusing.
Questions: Did BAGEL-7B-FT receive the exact same total data and training compute as Omni-View (i.e., including the 61k re10k clips) but with only the understanding objective? If not, how do you disentangle the performance gain from additional generation data versus the proposed architecture/objectives?

What exactly is the 'VSI-Bench (subset)' used in the ablations? Is it the full VSI-Bench test set, a separate validation set, or a randomly sampled subset? If it is the test set, how do you avoid overfitting through repeated ablations?

How are gradients from the texture-module loss (L_tex) and geometry-module loss (L_geo) backpropagated to the understanding model? Are there any stop-gradient operations, especially given the flow-matching and diffusion-forcing training?

Can you provide a quantitative evaluation of the geometry module's depth and camera-pose prediction accuracy on a standard benchmark (e.g., Re10k depth/pose metrics)? Without this, it is hard to assess the role of 'explicit geometric constraints.'
What are the exact train/test splits for SQA3D, ScanQA, ScanRefer, and 3DOD used in training? Were any validation or test scenes from these benchmarks included in the 780k training data?
Limitations: The paper acknowledges that grounding capabilities are not substantiated and that the geometry module relies on synthetic depth maps, which may limit real-world geometric accuracy.
The main claim that generation facilitates understanding is confounded by the use of additional generation data in Omni-View compared to the BAGEL-7B-FT baseline.
The model's generation is currently limited to short sequences (25 frames) and lacks long-range world generation capabilities.
The paper does not report computational resource requirements (GPU-hours, memory) or inference speed, which limits practical reproducibility.
No analysis of failure modes in complex real-world scenes is provided beyond a single qualitative bad case.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: Omni-View is a unified multimodal model for 3D scenes that jointly performs scene understanding, novel view synthesis, and geometry estimation. Built on BAGEL, it separates the generation model into a texture module (for novel view RGB synthesis via flow matching and autoregressive generation) and a geometry module (for depth map and camera pose estimation), and introduces a two-stage training strategy: stage 1 jointly trains understanding, texture, and geometry (with dense-to-sparse reference image scheduling), and stage 2 fine-tunes generation with RGB-depth-pose joint learning. The model achieves state-of-the-art 55.4 on VSI-Bench, strong results on 3D QA/localization benchmarks, and competitive performance in single-view novel view synthesis and scene generation, all while using only RGB input.
Strengths: The core idea of leveraging generation (novel view synthesis and geometry estimation) to improve 3D scene understanding is novel and well-motivated, with clear connections to neurocognitive evidence.
The architecture design that splits generation into texture and geometry modules, and the two-stage training with dense-to-sparse curriculum, are thoughtful and supported by ablations.

Empirical results are strong: Omni-View outperforms specialized 3D understanding models on VSI-Bench (55.4 avg) and shows significant gains in relative distance and appearance order, tasks requiring spatiotemporal and geometric reasoning.
The model operates on RGB-only input, making it more practical than methods that require explicit 3D input (voxels, point clouds, BEVs).
Ablation studies validate the contribution of each module, autoregressive generation, and D2S schedule, providing useful insights.
Weaknesses: The paper lacks sufficient implementation details for reproducibility: exact architectures of the texture/geometry modules, how features are extracted from the understanding model, how depth noise is decoded to depth maps, and the camera pose decoder are described vaguely.

The training data composition is underspecified: the 780k understanding items are simply listed as sourced from multiple datasets, but no filtering criteria or distribution details are provided; the 61k video clips for generation are also not clearly described.

The comparisons may be unfair or uncontrolled: BAGEL-FT (the primary unified baseline) does not have the geometry module, so Omni-View has extra parameters; VSI-Bench baselines come from different papers with different inference settings and are not consistently evaluated.
The paper relies on synthetic depth maps (from Voyager pipeline) for geometry supervision, which could limit real-world geometry accuracy; the authors admit this but do not quantify its impact.

Presentation quality is poor: there are numerous typos, grammatical errors, unclear equations (e.g., Eq. 1 refers to 'provided texture noise' when the model predicts noise), and corrupted table formatting (e.g., Table 1 headers have stray pipes and color codes).
The claim of 'state-of-the-art' on VSI-Bench is not backed by a clear comparison to the previous best score or specification of the exact evaluation protocol.
The scene generation evaluation uses Dust3R to reconstruct generated videos, which may not fully capture 3D consistency, and the paper admits camera-pose control is challenging.
Questions: How exactly is the autoregressive generation ordered in the texture module? Does it generate frames in temporal order and how are previous generated frames fed back as conditions?
What is the precise implementation of 'diffusion forcing' in training the texture module?
In the geometry module, how is the predicted depth noise mapped back to a depth map? What is the architecture of the camera pose decoder (is it a simple MLP)?
How is the dense-to-sparse (D2S) schedule implemented? Is the decrease in reference images stepwise based on iterations, and what are the exact steps?
What hyperparameters are used in ablation studies (e.g., number of training iterations, batch size, learning rate)?
Why does the geometry module, which uses synthetic depth, still improve understanding on relative distance? Does this improvement transfer to real-world depth estimation?
Are the VSI-Bench baselines evaluated using the same frame numbers (8-32) and 640p resolution? If not, which results are taken from original papers?
What is the previous state-of-the-art on VSI-Bench for context? The paper does not state prior numbers.
Since Omni-View has a larger parameter count than BAGEL-FT (due to the geometry module), how do the authors ensure the performance gain is due to the generation mechanism rather than model capacity?
Limitations: The geometry module is trained with synthetic depth maps, which may not generalize to diverse real-world scenes and limits the accuracy of geometry estimation.
The model is limited to short-range generation; it cannot produce long, consistent 3D world sequences.
3D visual grounding (e.g., referring object localization) is not evaluated, and the paper notes this as future work.
The paper does not analyze failure cases in understanding tasks; only an NVS failure case is shown in the appendix.
The model is fixed at 7B scale; no experiments explore scaling to larger model sizes or the effect on performance.
Potential negative societal impacts include misuse of 3D scene generation for creating deceptive or malicious content, as acknowledged in the ethics statement.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper presents Omni-View, a unified multimodal model for 3D scene understanding and generation based on multiview images. It extends the Bagel architecture by splitting the generation model into a texture module (novel view synthesis) and a geometry module (depth and camera pose estimation), and trains the whole system in two stages: first jointly for understanding and generation with a dense-to-sparse reference image curriculum, then finetunes the generation modules while freezing the understanding model. The model achieves 55.4 on VSI-Bench, outperforming prior specialized and unified models without explicit 3D input, and also shows competitive performance on 3D QA, localization, novel view synthesis, and scene generation.
Strengths: The paper explores a meaningful paradigm of using generative tasks (NVS and geometry estimation) to improve 3D scene understanding, with ablations showing that both texture and geometry modules contribute to understanding gains.

The proposed architecture with separate texture and geometry modules allows explicit geometric supervision and spatiotemporal modeling, yielding substantial improvements on VSI-Bench (55.4 vs. 46.3 for BAGEL-FT) and competitive results on SQA3D and ScanQA.
The dense-to-sparse (D2S) curriculum in stage 1 is a simple yet effective training strategy, and ablation shows it outperforms dense-only, sparse-only, and random masking.

The method demonstrates that a unified understanding-generation model can approach or exceed specialized 3D understanding models without relying on explicit 3D input, which has practical applicability.
The authors plan to release code and weights, which would help reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The paper is poorly written with many typos, grammatical errors, and LaTeX artifacts (e.g., 'forzen', 'piror', 'Experience', 'donate', table formatting issues), making it difficult to follow in places.

The architecture description is vague: the exact information flow between understanding model, texture module, and geometry module is not fully specified, and the equations contain formatting errors that obscure the formulations.

The geometry module is trained with synthetic depth maps from Voyager, which lack absolute metric scale; the authors admit this limits absolute distance estimation, and the depth prediction quality is not rigorously evaluated.

The generation results show only marginal improvements over existing scene generation models (e.g., PSNR 23.22 vs. 23.12 for Voyager), yet the paper claims state-of-the-art without statistical significance tests.
The experimental setup omits critical details: exact hyperparameters, dataset filtering criteria, computational cost, and the number of training steps are not provided, hurting reproducibility.
The comparison baselines for unified models are limited to BAGEL-FT; no other recent unified models (e.g., Janus, Chameleon) are compared on the same tasks.
The ablations are limited and do not analyze the interaction between stages, the effect of camera pose loss weight, or the sensitivity of the D2S schedule.
The evaluation uses a non-standard protocol for scene generation (Dust3R reconstruction), which may not be comparable with prior work and introduces additional variability.
Questions: How are the reference images selected in the texture module during training and inference? Is the camera pose for novel views provided as input or predicted?
What is the total computational cost (GPU hours, number of parameters) of Omni-View compared to BAGEL-FT?
Why is the geometry module not conditioned on understanding model features in stage 2? Does this cause a distribution shift that affects depth/pose accuracy?
Can you elaborate on the 'diffusion forcing' used in the texture module? How is it applied and what is its contribution?
The loss weights in stage 1 are set to 1, 1, 0.1 for understanding, texture, and geometry. Were these tuned? How sensitive are the results to these weights?
How were the 61k video clips selected from re10k? What is the overlap between the generation training data and the understanding training data?
In Table 4, the unified texture+geometry architecture performs worse than the separate modules. What is the suspected reason for this?
Limitations: The geometry module's depth prediction is trained on synthetic depth maps and may not be accurate in real-world scenes, limiting absolute metric understanding.
The model currently lacks 3D visual grounding capabilities and cannot perform long-range world generation, as acknowledged by the authors.
The method requires multiview images as input, which may not be available in many practical applications.
The evaluation is largely confined to indoor scenes (SQA3D, ScanQA, ScanRefer, Re10k); generalization to outdoor or dynamic scenes is unclear.
Potential negative societal impact: 3D scene generation could be misused to create deceptive or malicious virtual environments, though the authors include an ethics statement.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: Omni-View is a unified 3D scene understanding and generation model built on BAGEL-7B. It splits the generation process into a texture module for novel view synthesis and a geometry module for depth and camera pose estimation, with the goal that generating 3D structure improves 3D understanding. It is trained in two stages: stage 1 jointly trains understanding, texture, and geometry; stage 2 fine-tunes generation with RGB-Depth-Pose joint learning. The model achieves SOTA 55.4 on VSI-Bench and strong performance on novel view synthesis.
Strengths: Novel architecture that decomposes generation into texture and geometry modules, explicitly demonstrating that generative modeling of 3D structure can improve scene understanding and spatial reasoning.
Strong empirical results, particularly on VSI-Bench (55.4), outperforming specialized 3D understanding models while remaining applicable without explicit 3D input.
Comprehensive ablation studies that validate the contribution of each module and training strategy component.
Unified model handles both understanding and generation, narrowing the gap between unified and specialized models in several benchmarks.
Weaknesses: The claim that 'generation facilitates understanding' is not fully supported because the added re10k video data may itself boost understanding; there is no control experiment training on the same data without generation objectives.

Several implementation details are missing, including exact architecture dimensions, flow matching sampling specifics, camera pose embedding details, dataset sizes, and hyperparameters beyond a few basic choices, hindering reproducibility.

The paper contains numerous typos, formatting errors, and grammar issues (e.g., 'Archtitectures', 'forzen', 'piror', 'randon mask', 'understandimg'), and some tables have missing values, reducing professional clarity.

The geometry module is trained on pseudo-depth maps from the Voyager pipeline, which may be inaccurate, yet no direct evaluation of depth/pose prediction quality is provided to contextualize its impact on understanding.
The relationship between camera poses provided to the texture module and those estimated by the geometry module is not clearly explained, creating a conceptual gap in the architecture.
Questions: In Table 1, BAGEL-7B-FT is fine-tuned with the same understanding data but without the re10k generation data; could the improvements from Omni-View be attributed to simply seeing more video data rather than the generation objective? Did you run a control with re10k data under an understanding-only loss?
How are the 'specified camera poses' for the texture module obtained at inference? For single-view NVS, are these poses ground-truth from the test set, and how is the trajectory determined?

review.Summary: Omni-View is a unified multimodal model for 3D scene understanding and generation. It extends Bagel by splitting the generation branch into a texture module (novel view synthesis via flow matching) and a geometry module (depth and camera pose estimation), and integrates these with the understanding model. Training proceeds in two stages: joint training of understanding and generation, then generation fine-tuning. The model achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench and strong performance on 3D QA and generation benchmarks.
Strengths: The concept of using generative tasks (novel view synthesis and geometry estimation) to improve 3D understanding is novel and well-motivated by human cognition.
The split into texture and geometry modules is a clean architectural design that allows the model to explicitly learn spatiotemporal and geometric features.
The two-stage training with dense-to-sparse reference views is an interesting curriculum that yields significant gains.
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate the contribution of each component (texture, geometry, autoregressive generation, D2S, stage 2).
Strong empirical results on VSI-Bench (55.4) and 3D understanding benchmarks, outperforming tailored models without 3D input.
Generation quality also improves over unified baselines.
Weaknesses: The paper is poorly written with numerous typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'Archtitectures', 'forzen', 'piror') and inconsistent formatting, which significantly hampers readability.

Technical details are insufficient for reproducibility: the architecture is not fully described (e.g., how the understanding model features are cross-attended, the exact structure of the geometry module, camera pose query mechanism), and equations are not properly typeset.

The geometry module's accuracy is not directly evaluated; only indirect effects on understanding are shown. Without metrics for depth/pose estimation, it's unclear if the geometry module fulfills its intended function.

The claim that 'generation facilitates understanding' is only demonstrated through joint training, but the computational overhead and data usage increase may confound the results. The baseline BAGEL-FT is fine-tuned on understanding data only, which is a reasonable control, but the paper does not isolate the effect of generation data alone.
The model uses synthetic depth maps from Voyager for training, which may limit the accuracy of geometry estimation and the real-world generalization.
No analysis of failure cases or limitations of the generation model (e.g., camera pose control issues are mentioned but not studied).

The paper does not provide code or model weights, and the reproducibility statement is generic without sufficient experimental detail (e.g., hyperparameters for flow matching, diffusion forcing specifics).
The comparison in Table 3 shows only marginal improvements in NVS over specialized models, and the paper admits pixel-level fidelity is only slightly improved, but the significance is not tested.
Questions: How exactly are the understanding model's features integrated into the geometry module via cross-attention? What are the dimensions and layer choices?
What is the schedule for the dense-to-sparse reference reduction? Is it linear, stepwise, etc.?
Why is λ_geo set to 0.1? Was it tuned? What is the sensitivity?
How does the model handle camera pose estimation during inference? Is the pose query learned and fixed?
Since the geometry module uses synthetic depth maps, what is the impact on real-world geometry prediction? Are there any experiments on real depth?
What is the computational cost of the two-stage training? How many total training steps/epochs?
Does stage 2 fine-tuning affect the understanding performance? If so, is there degradation?
Limitations: The geometry module's depth prediction relies on synthetic data, limiting real-world accuracy.
The generation model is limited to 25 frames and cannot generate long-range sequences.
The model's grounding (referring to objects with bounding boxes) is not evaluated, as noted in the paper.
The paper does not analyze the model's performance under varying number of input views.
The lack of code and detailed hyperparameters hinders reproducibility.

review.Summary: Omni-View is a unified multimodal model for 3D scenes that jointly performs scene understanding, novel view synthesis, and geometry estimation. Built on BAGEL-7B, it splits generation into a texture module (RGB novel view synthesis via flow matching and autoregressive generation) and a geometry module (depth and camera pose estimation), and trains the full system in two stages: a joint understanding-and-generation stage with a dense-to-sparse reference-view curriculum, followed by a generation-focused fine-tuning stage. The model achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench (55.4) and strong performance on 3D QA/localization benchmarks, while also demonstrating competitive novel view synthesis and scene generation, all from RGB-only input.
Strengths: The core idea of leveraging generation (novel view synthesis and geometry estimation) to improve 3D scene understanding is novel and well-motivated, connecting to neurocognitive evidence.
The split into separate texture and geometry modules is a thoughtful architectural design that enables explicit geometric supervision and autoregressive spatiotemporal modeling.
The dense-to-sparse (D2S) reference-view curriculum is a simple yet effective training strategy, with ablations showing clear benefits over dense-only, sparse-only, and random masking.

Strong empirical results: Omni-View substantially outperforms the BAGEL-FT baseline on VSI-Bench (55.4 vs. 46.3) and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art results on 3D understanding benchmarks without explicit 3D input.
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 4-7) decompose the contributions of texture/geometry modules, autoregressive generation, D2S schedule, and stage 2, providing useful insights.
The model operates on RGB-only input, making it more practical than methods that require point clouds, voxels, or BEV representations.
Weaknesses: A major confound exists in the main comparison: BAGEL-7B-FT is trained on understanding data only, while Omni-View also uses 61k additional video clips from Re10k for generation. The reported gains could stem from extra data/compute rather than the 'generation facilitates understanding' mechanism; no control experiment trains on the same added data with only an understanding objective.
Model-size mismatch in comparisons: several strong baselines (e.g., VG-LLM-4B, Spatial-MLLM-4B) have 4B parameters, while Omni-View is 7B, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art status.

The geometry module's actual depth and camera-pose prediction accuracy is never directly evaluated on standard benchmarks. Since training uses synthetic depth maps from Voyager, the contribution of 'explicit geometric constraints' is not validated, and the limited ablation shows only modest improvements in absolute distance tasks.

The paper is poorly written with numerous typos, grammatical errors, and LaTeX artifacts (e.g., 'forzen', 'randon mask', 'donate', 'Archtitectures', broken equations, garbled table formatting), which significantly hampers clarity and reproducibility.

Missing technical details: exact architectures of texture/geometry modules, cross-attention mechanism, flow-matching formulation, diffusion-forcing specifics, camera pose query, dataset filtering criteria, and hyperparameters are not fully specified.
The VSI-Bench subset used in ablations is not clearly defined; if it overlaps with the test set, repeated ablations could lead to overfitting.

The paper claims state-of-the-art in scene generation, but Table 3 shows only marginal improvements over specialized models (e.g., PSNR 23.22 vs. 23.12 for Voyager), with no statistical significance tests; text is even contradictory about the extent of improvement.
The generation evaluation uses a non-standard protocol (Dust3R reconstruction) that may not be fully comparable with prior work, and the paper admits camera-pose control is challenging.
Questions: Did BAGEL-7B-FT receive the exact same total data and training compute as Omni-View (including the 61k re10k clips) but with only the understanding objective? If not, how do you disentangle the performance gain from additional generation data versus the proposed architecture/objectives?

What exactly is the 'VSI-Bench (subset)' used in ablations? Is it the full test set, a separate validation set, or a random sample? If it overlaps with the test set, how do you avoid overfitting through repeated ablations?
How are the understanding model's features integrated into the texture and geometry modules? Provide precise architecture details (dimensions, cross-attention layers, conditioning mechanisms).
What is the flow-matching formulation: number of sampling steps, noise parameterization, how autoregressive conditioning is applied across frames, and what 'diffusion forcing' concretely involves?

How are the camera poses used in the texture module obtained during training and inference? Are they ground-truth, predicted by the geometry module, or specified externally? What is the relationship between the pose used for NVS and the pose estimated by the geometry module?

Can you provide quantitative evaluation of the geometry module's depth and camera-pose prediction accuracy on standard benchmarks (e.g., Re10k or ScanNet depth/pose metrics)? Without this, it is hard to assess the role of 'explicit geometric constraints.'
What are the exact hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, training steps, loss weights) and computational cost (GPU hours) for Omni-View and BAGEL-FT?
Why does the geometry module, trained on synthetic depth, still improve understanding on relative distance? Does this improvement transfer to real-world depth estimation?
How was the 780k understanding data composed and filtered? What is the distribution across datasets? Are any validation or test scenes from SQA3D/ScanQA/ScanRefer included in training?
In Table 4, the unified texture+geometry architecture performs worse than separate modules. What is the suspected reason and what architectural changes would recover performance?
Why is λ_geo set to 0.1? What is the sensitivity of results to this weight?
Does stage 2 fine-tuning affect understanding performance? If so, is there degradation or improvement?
Limitations: The geometry module relies on synthetic depth maps from the Voyager pipeline, which lack absolute metric scale and may not generalize to real-world scenes, limiting absolute distance estimation and real-world geometric accuracy.
The model is limited to short-range generation (25 frames) and cannot produce long, consistent 3D world sequences.
3D visual grounding (e.g., referring object localization) is not evaluated, and the paper notes this as future work.
The paper does not analyze failure modes in complex real-world scenes beyond a single qualitative bad case.
The method requires multiview images as input, which may not be available in many practical scenarios.
Evaluation is largely confined to indoor scenes (Re10k, ScanNet, SQA3D); generalization to outdoor or dynamic scenes is unclear.

The main claim that generation facilitates understanding is confounded by the addition of extra video data in Omni-View compared to BAGEL-FT, so the true effect of generative objectives is not isolated.
No analysis of computational resource requirements (GPU-hours, memory, inference speed) is provided, hindering practical reproducibility.
Potential negative societal impacts are acknowledged only generically, with no concrete discussion of safeguards against synthetic scene misuse or biases.

The paper is poorly written with numerous typos, grammatical errors, and LaTeX artifacts (e.g., 'forzen', 'randon mask', 'donate', 'Archtitectures', broken equations, garbled table formatting), which significantly hampers clarity and reproducibility.

Missing technical details: exact architectures of texture/geometry modules, cross-attention mechanism, flow-matching formulation, diffusion-forcing specifics, camera pose query, dataset filtering criteria, and hyperparameters are not fully specified.
The VSI-Bench subset used in ablations is not clearly defined; if it overlaps with the test set, repeated ablations could lead to overfitting.

The paper claims state-of-the-art in scene generation, but Table 3 shows only marginal improvements over specialized models (e.g., PSNR 23.22 vs. 23.12 for Voyager), with no statistical significance tests; text is even contradictory about the extent of improvement.
The generation evaluation uses a non-standard protocol (Dust3R reconstruction) that may not be fully comparable with prior work, and the paper admits camera-pose control is challenging.
Questions: Did BAGEL-7B-FT receive the exact same total data and training compute as Omni-View (including the 61k re10k clips) but with only the understanding objective? If not, how do you disentangle the performance gain from additional generation data versus the proposed architecture/objectives?

What exactly is the 'VSI-Bench (subset)' used in ablations? Is it the full test set, a separate validation set, or a random sample? If it overlaps with the test set, how do you avoid overfitting through repeated ablations?
How are the understanding model's features integrated into the texture and geometry modules? Provide precise architecture details (dimensions, cross-attention layers, conditioning mechanisms).
What is the flow-matching formulation: number of sampling steps, noise parameterization, how autoregressive conditioning is applied across frames, and what 'diffusion forcing' concretely involves?

How are the camera poses used in the texture module obtained during training and inference? Are they ground-truth, predicted by the geometry module, or specified externally? What is the relationship between the pose used for NVS and the pose estimated by the geometry module?

Can you provide quantitative evaluation of the geometry module's depth and camera-pose prediction accuracy on standard benchmarks (e.g., Re10k or ScanNet depth/pose metrics)? Without this, it is hard to assess the role of 'explicit geometric constraints.'
What are the exact hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, training steps, loss weights) and computational cost (GPU hours) for Omni-View and BAGEL-FT?
Why does the geometry module, trained on synthetic depth, still improve understanding on relative distance? Does this improvement transfer to real-world depth estimation?
How was the 780k understanding data composed and filtered? What is the distribution across datasets? Are any validation or test scenes from SQA3D/ScanQA/ScanRefer included in training?
In Table 4, the unified texture+geometry architecture performs worse than separate modules. What is the suspected reason and what architectural changes would recover performance?
Why is λ_geo set to 0.1? What is the sensitivity of results to this weight?
Does stage 2 fine-tuning affect understanding performance? If so, is there degradation or improvement?
Limitations: The geometry module relies on synthetic depth maps from the Voyager pipeline, which lack absolute metric scale and may not generalize to real-world scenes, limiting absolute distance estimation and real-world geometric accuracy.
The model is limited to short-range generation (25 frames) and cannot produce long, consistent 3D world sequences.
3D visual grounding (e.g., referring object localization) is not evaluated, and the paper notes this as future work.
The paper does not analyze failure modes in complex real-world scenes beyond a single qualitative bad case.
The method requires multiview images as input, which may not be available in many practical scenarios.
Evaluation is largely confined to indoor scenes (Re10k, ScanNet, SQA3D); generalization to outdoor or dynamic scenes is unclear.

The main claim that generation facilitates understanding is confounded by the addition of extra video data in Omni-View compared to BAGEL-FT, so the true effect of generative objectives is not isolated.
No analysis of computational resource requirements (GPU-hours, memory, inference speed) is provided, hindering practical reproducibility.
Potential negative societal impacts are acknowledged only generically, with no concrete discussion of safeguards against synthetic scene misuse or biases.
